blocks.text: Chapter 1.
Optimal Stopping: The 37% Rule

Come in, friend — new fire, new book, and this one is a strange delight: it claims the computer scientists have been quietly solving your problems all along. When to stop looking for an apartment. When to take the job. Even whom to marry. Tonight we start with that last one — and with a broken-hearted astronomer.

The year is 1611. Johannes Kepler — the man who mapped the orbits of the planets — has lost his wife to cholera. In time he resolves to remarry, and being Kepler, he goes about it methodically: over two years he courts eleven women, one after another, tormented the entire time by a single question. Settle for this one? Or keep looking — and risk losing her while chasing someone better who may not exist? He wrote of a heart that "held itself back" while options remained.
Kepler's agony has a name now, friend. And — astonishingly — it has an exact mathematical answer.
The secretary problem

Mathematicians call it the secretary problem: you interview applicants one at a time, in random order. After each, you must hire or reject on the spot — no going back. And you can only judge each candidate relative to those you've already seen — there's no absolute scale. You want the single best person in the pool. Stop too early and you probably haven't met the best yet. Wait too long and you've probably already rejected them. Every sensible strategy, it turns out, takes a Look-Then-Leap shape: first a phase of pure calibration — gathering data, committing to no one — then commit to the first option that beats everyone from the look phase. The only question is where the crossover falls.

Pause and guess: The mathematics pins the answer to a precise, almost mystical number. What percentage of your options should you look at before you start leaping — and what are your odds of landing the very best?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Look at exactly 37% — then leap at the first option better than everything you've seen. And here's the eerie part, friend: follow the rule and your chance of landing the single best candidate is... also 37%. The two numbers coincide because both equal 1/e — Euler's number, hiding in your love life. It holds no matter how large the pool: the best of 100 applicants is a 1-in-100 shot by dumb luck, but the algorithm delivers better than 1-in-3 — and no strategy on Earth can do better. Yes, that's a 63% failure rate — and it's optimal; every rival intuition (grab early, always hold out) does worse as the pool grows. The rule converts cleanly to time, too: a month allotted to apartment hunting means eleven days of pure looking, then take the first place that beats everything so far. And life's variants bend the number, friend: if your offers can be rejected half the time, start leaping at 25%; if you can go back to passed-over options with even a coin-flip chance they'll still have you, look until 61%. Kepler lived that last one — he went back to candidate number five, Susanna Reuttinger, who said yes, and the marriage was by all accounts a happy one. Mathematician Michael Trick wasn't so lucky: he ran the 37% rule on his dating life, found the first-best-yet woman, proposed... and was refused. Know which variant you're actually in before you trust its number.
When you know the score

Everything above assumes you learn only rankings — best-so-far or not — which is why the look phase exists at all: you need data before a standard can. But sometimes life hands you an objective score. A typist whose words-per-minute test places her at an exact percentile means something from applicant one — a 95th-percentile typist is excellent whether she's first or fiftieth. With full information, the strategy changes shape entirely: no look phase — a Threshold Rule. Accept immediately anyone who clears a percentile bar, and lower the bar as options dwindle: with many candidates left, hold out for the top few percent; with one left, take what comes. And full information pays, friend: the threshold player lands the best option 58% of the time — smashing through the 37% ceiling. The broader lesson: before resigning yourself to the ranking game, hunt for a yardstick — market data, salary ranges, test scores. Any objective standard converts "compare against what I've seen" into "compare against the world" — and nearly doubles your odds.

Once searching itself costs something, thresholds rule everyday life. Selling a house: keep waiting only while the expected gain from one more offer exceeds the cost of waiting for it — and strikingly, with an endless stream of buyers, the right threshold doesn't depend on how long you've searched. Set it in advance from the waiting cost, and never sell below it, no matter how tired you get. Parking is the same game keyed to occupancy: at 99% full, grab the first spot nearly seventy spaces out; on an emptier street, cruise closer. Even quitting while ahead has a formula: a burglar who succeeds with probability p on each job should retire after about p/(1−p) heists — a 90% success rate justifies about nine jobs; a 50% rate justifies exactly one. And some games — triple-or-nothing — have no optimal stopping point at all: the math never says stop... which is the math's way of saying never sit down.
The almost-rational impatience
So how do real humans play, friend? In 1997, researchers Darryl Seale and Amnon Rapoport ran the classic secretary problem on live subjects.
Pause and guess: Most people did use Look-Then-Leap — the right SHAPE of strategy. But they got the crossover wrong, in one consistent direction. Which way — and were they simply being foolish?
Ready? Here is what happened.

They leapt too early — around 31% instead of 37% — and across study after study, the signature repeats: people stop searching too soon, leaving the best options unseen. But here's the twist that redeems us, friend: the textbook problem assumes searching is free. Real searching never is — every interview, apartment viewing, and first date burns time and effort. And when Seale and Rapoport re-ran the math charging even a small cost per candidate inspected, the optimal strategy shifted to earlier stopping — closely matching what people actually do. Our impatience may be a rational response to a time cost the classical model forgot, not a defect in our heads. The practical synthesis: know which world you're in — rankings or scores, rejection or recall, cheap search or costly — then set your leap point or threshold in advance. The mathematics exists precisely because the in-the-moment question — "is this good enough, or is better coming?" — is exactly where human judgment flounders. When to stop looking isn't a matter of temperament, friend. For a surprising range of life's problems, it has a provably best answer.
Before you go

So: Kepler's eleven candidates and the heart that held itself back; the 37% rule, where 1/e sets both the look phase and the odds; rejection moves the leap to 25%, recall stretches it to 61%, and a real yardstick nearly doubles your chances; thresholds govern houses, parking spots, and retiring burglars; and our too-early leaps turn out to be almost rational after all. This week, friend: pick one open search in your life, fix the pool or the clock, and mark the 37% line before you look again.

But a harder question hides beneath tonight's, friend. Stopping assumes you're hunting for one best thing. What about the choices you make over and over — the restaurant tonight, and next week, and the week after? Every dinner is a bet: the beloved old reliable... or the unknown new place that might become your favorite? Computer scientists call it the explore/exploit tradeoff, they solved it with slot machines, and the answer depends on something you'd never guess: how much time you have left. Next time: explore versus exploit — new favorite, or old reliable?
Key takeaways
Sequential no-going-back choices have a provably best strategy: look at 37% purely to calibrate, then leap at the first best-yet option.
37% is 1/e — and it's also your success odds; no strategy beats it, and a 63% failure rate is still the ceiling.
Variants shift the number: possible rejection → leap at 25%; possible recall → look until 61% (Kepler's happy ending).
Objective yardsticks change the game: a percentile Threshold Rule wins 58% of the time — hunt for scores before settling for rankings.
When search costs, set thresholds in advance — house prices, parking distance, even the burglar's p/(1−p) retirement rule.
Humans leap at ~31%: almost rational once search costs count — but audit your early grabs when looking is genuinely cheap.
